Now let me compile the verse-by-verse notes from all the sources I've gathered.

---

## Exodus 27 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

### Outline

The chapter has three sections:
- **vv. 1–8**: The Bronze Altar (Altar of Burnt Offering)
- **vv. 9–19**: The Courtyard of the Tabernacle
- **vv. 20–21**: The Oil for the Lampstand

*(Outline adapted from David Guzik, used also at Precept Austin)*
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-27/ ; https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-27-commentary

---

### v. 1 — The Bronze Altar: Dimensions and Materials

**"You are to build an altar of acacia wood. The altar must be square, five cubits long, five cubits wide, and three cubits high."**

- **Gill (Baptist, 1771):** The Hebrew says "the altar," implying it is the one definitive altar for burnt offerings, distinct from the earlier altar of earth (Ex 20:24) and from the altar of incense (Ex 30:1). It was placed in the open court so that smoke could ascend freely. Gill insists the altar is **not** a type of the heart, nor of the Lord's Table, nor of the cross, but **of Christ Himself** — specifically, His divine nature is the altar that supports and sanctifies the sacrifice of His human nature (citing Heb 13:10). The acacia wood (incorruptible) typifies Christ's enduring nature; the square shape denotes the perfection and permanence of His sacrifice. The height of three cubits (about 4.5 ft) was practical, so a man of ordinary height (about 4 cubits) could minister at it. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/exodus-27.html

- **Ellicott (Anglican, 1878):** The Hebrew reads "the altar" — worship without sacrifice was unknown, so a sanctuary required an altar. The acacia wood seems to conflict with Ex 20:24-25 (altars of earth or unhewn stone), but Jewish commentators (Jarchi, Kalisch) explain that this was an **"altar-case,"** to be filled with earth at each encampment. The height of three cubits was practical; a greater height would have hindered arranging victims. If perfection of form were the only concern, the altar would have been a cube. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/exodus-27.html

- **Guzik (evangelical/charismatic):** The Hebrew word for "altar" essentially means **"killing-place"** — a place of death and sacrifice where atonement was made. Under the new covenant, our "killing-place" (altar) is the cross (Heb 13:10). Dimensions: 7.5 ft square × 4.5 ft high. The bronze overlay enabled it to survive high temperatures. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-27/

- **Precept Austin (evangelical, citing multiple sources):** The altar was twice as long as the mercy seat and over three times as wide, showing that shed blood is paramount to accessing God's grace and mercy. The square shape contrasted with pagan altars (round or triangular). The definite article "the altar" identifies it as the main high altar. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-27-commentary

- **Coffman (Church of Christ):** The bronze altar dominated the entrance; it symbolizes Christ's atoning death. Bronze speaks of divine judgment (cf. Num 21:9; Jn 3:14; Rev 1:15). At Calvary Christ met "the burning heat of divine justice against sin." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/exodus-27.html

- **NET Bible notes:** The top of the altar is not described; some suggest it was filled with earth when in use. This portable frame was an improvement over the field altar, but the purpose remained: worshipers made sacrifices to find forgiveness and atonement. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-27-commentary

---

### v. 2 — The Four Horns and Bronze Overlay

**"Make a horn on each of its four corners, so that the horns are of one piece, and overlay it with bronze."**

- **Ellicott:** Horns were, so far as is known, **peculiar to Israelite altars**. They began as ornaments but came to be regarded as the most sacred part — the virtue of the altar was thought to lie in them. Victims were bound to them (Ps 118:27); criminals clung to them for asylum (1 Ki 1:50; 2:28); blood of sin offerings was smeared on them (Ex 29:12; Lev 8:15). They were to be of one piece with the altar, not attached separately. The bronze overlay was necessary to prevent the wood from burning. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/exodus-27.html

- **Gill:** Horns denote the power of Christ, who is "the horn of salvation," preserving His people and protecting those who fly to Him for refuge. The four corners may represent the four parts of the world from which souls come to Christ. The bronze overlay signifies Christ's strength in bearing the fire of divine wrath. Jarchi noted the bronze atoned for "the impudence of the forehead, which is as brass" (Isa 48:4). — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/exodus-27.html

- **Guzik:** Horns show the altar "reaching out" to all directions; they display strength and power. Atoning blood was applied to each horn. They were also used to bind the sacrificial animals (Ps 118:27). The altar's bronze sides became rough and scarred after the censers of Korah's rebellion were hammered onto them (Num 16:38-40) — a permanent memorial of judgment against rebellion. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-27/

- **NET Bible notes:** The horns were indispensable — the most sacred part. Blood was put on them; fugitives could cling to them; priests grasped them in intercessory prayer. They signified power (as animal horns do) and may also represent the sacrificial animals killed on the altar. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-27-commentary

- **Cambridge Bible for Schools and Colleges:** The origin of the horn symbolism is uncertain. The most probable theory (Evans, Robertson Smith) is that horns are conventionalized representations of the horns of sacrificed oxen, set before the deity. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/exodus/27.htm

---

### v. 3 — The Bronze Utensils

**"Make all its utensils of bronze—its pots for removing ashes, its shovels, its sprinkling bowls, its meat forks, and its firepans."**

- **Ellicott:** The "pans" were scuttles for ash removal (the rare Hebrew word implies unburnt fat mixed with ashes). "Shovels" for clearing ashes, "basins" for receiving and sprinkling blood (Ex 24:6), "fleshhooks" (three-pronged) for arranging the pieces on the altar, and "firepans" (elsewhere "snuffdishes" or "censers") for carrying embers from the brazen altar to the altar of incense (Lev 16:12). — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/exodus-27.html

- **Gill:** The pans gathered ashes for removal; this was done every morning about cock-crowing. The "basins" were sprinkling bowls for blood. The flesh hooks were recurved to turn flesh on the coals. The firepans were censers to carry coals to the incense altar. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/exodus-27.html

- **Guzik (citing Kaiser):** Pans held fat-soaked ashes; basins caught blood for sprinkling on the altar's base; forks (three-pronged) arranged the sacrifice or retrieved the priest's portion (1 Sam 2:13); firepans carried fire to the incense altar (Lev 10:1; 16:12). All these were specially made and set apart for tabernacle service. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-27/

- **Precept Austin (citing Thompson):** Ash pots received and stored ashes; fire pans held and transported live coals; shovels removed ashes and reconfigured hot coals; bowls contained liquid and caught draining blood; forks handled the meat. All utensils are plural, indicating more than one of each. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-27-commentary

---

### v. 4 — The Bronze Grating and Rings

**"Construct for it a grate of bronze mesh, and make a bronze ring at each of the four corners of the mesh."**

- **Ellicott:** The position of the grating is uncertain. One view: it reached from the middle of the altar to its base and protected the sides from the priests' feet. Another: it surrounded the upper part to catch falling portions of victims. The rings were for carrying poles, as with the ark and table (Ex 25:12, 26). — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/exodus-27.html

- **Gill:** The grate was a bronze sieve or network (cf. Amos 9:9), the hearth on which the sacrifice and wood were laid and burnt. The holes let blood or ashes drain through. This typifies the purity of Christ's sacrifice. The rings at the four corners were for chains to fasten the grate to the four horns. Others think the rings were "by" the grate (not "in" it), on the sides of the altar for staves to carry it. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/exodus-27.html

- **Precept Austin (NET Note):** The Hebrew word for "grating" (mikbar) refers to a metal-work grate or network of bronze placed under the rim, midway from the bottom, on which burnt offerings were laid. The four rings at each corner were for poles. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-27-commentary

---

### v. 5 — Placement of the Grate

**"Set the grate beneath the ledge of the altar, so that the mesh comes halfway up the altar."**

- **Ellicott:** "Under the compass of the altar beneath" — was the "compass" the circumference at the top or a belt/step half-way up? The low height (4.5 ft) makes a step seem unnecessary, but the altar may have had a belt for ornament. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/exodus-27.html

- **Gill:** The grate was put within the hollow, square compass of the altar. The net reached to the midst (1.5 cubits from the ground, since the altar was 3 cubits high), allowing it to contain a great deal. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/exodus-27.html

- **Constable (Dallas Theological Seminary):** The grate was halfway to the ground inside the altar, allowing air to circulate under the sacrifices and ashes to fall below. The "ledge" projected out about halfway up. Perhaps priests stood on this ledge while placing offerings, or the ledge was on the inside to hold the grate. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/exodus-27.html (accessed via search excerpt)

- **Cambridge Bible:** Round the altar, midway between top and bottom, ran a projecting ledge — probably for the priests to stand upon when sacrificing — supported at its outer edge by a vertical grating of bronze that rested on the ground. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/exodus/27.htm

---

### vv. 6–7 — The Carrying Poles

**"Additionally, make poles of acacia wood for the altar and overlay them with bronze. The poles are to be inserted into the rings so that the poles are on two sides of the altar when it is carried."**

- **Gill:** The staves were like those made for the ark but overlaid with bronze, not gold. The rings were not those of the grate (which hung at the four corners on the horns) but rings on the sides of the altar itself. Being carried by the Levites typified ministers of the Gospel bearing the name of Christ and spreading the doctrine of His sacrifice throughout the world. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/exodus-27.html

- **Ellicott:** Like the ark and table, the altar needed rings and staves for transport when the Israelites changed camp. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/exodus-27.html

- **Guzik:** The grate also had the rings and poles for carrying the altar. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-27/

---

### v. 8 — Hollow Construction, Made According to the Pattern

**"Construct the altar with boards so that it is hollow. It is to be made just as you were shown on the mountain."**

- **Gill:** The hollowness made it light to carry. Jewish writers (Targum Jonathan) say the hollow was filled with dust and earth to match the altar of earth commanded earlier, but Gill rejects this — the hollowness was intentional. It may typify Christ emptying Himself (Phil 2:7): He "emptied himself, as it were, when he became incarnate, of all his greatness, glory, and riches." Moses was shown a model on the mount and was to ensure exact replication. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/exodus-27.html

- **Ellicott:** "Hollow with boards" — see the note on v.1 regarding the "altar-case" theory, where the hollow wooden case would be filled with earth. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/exodus-27.html

- **Constable:** The Book of Hebrews views this altar as a prototype of the better altar, which is Jesus Christ (Heb 13:10). — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/exodus-27.html

---

### v. 9 — The Courtyard: South Side

**"You are also to make a courtyard for the tabernacle. On the south side of the courtyard make curtains of finely spun linen, a hundred cubits long on one side."**

- **Ellicott:** Almost every ancient temple stood within a sacred enclosure isolating it from the common world. Egyptians particularly favoured oblong squares with a single entrance. An open court was essential since killing and burning victims in a covered space was intolerable. The Hebrew word for "hangings" is rare; the LXX renders it "sails," suggesting coarse sail-cloth woven with interstices through which activities inside could be seen. The court was open to all Israelites (Lev 1:3). — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/exodus-27.html

- **Gill:** The court typified the visible church on earth — an enclosure separated from the world, yet consisting of both real saints and hypocrites. The hangings were fine twined linen (six times twisted), not multi-coloured like the tabernacle curtains, but woven with eyelet holes so people could see through. This signifies that while only members partake of ordinances, outsiders may observe. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/exodus-27.html

- **Guzik (citing Kaiser):** The courtyard's purposes were fourfold: (1) a barrier preventing unlawful approach; (2) protection from wild animals; (3) a line of demarcation between the world and God's holy presence; (4) with its single gate, a way of approach to God. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-27/

- **Precept Austin (NET Note):** The courtyard is where the people gathered — they entered God's courts. Here sacrifices were made, choirs sang, believers offered praises, sins were forgiven, prayers were offered, holy days observed, and they heard from God. It was sacred because God met them there; they left the "world" and came into God's presence. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-27-commentary

---

### vv. 10–11 — Posts, Bases, Hooks, and Bands (South and North)

**"with twenty posts and twenty bronze bases, and silver hooks and bands on the posts. Likewise there are to be curtains on the north side..."**

- **Ellicott:** The pillars were of bronze (contra Kalisch who thought they were unplated wood); the Hebrew in Ex 27:10 and 38:10 confirms this. The "fillets" (bands) were connecting-rods uniting the pillars, helping support the hangings. Silver hooks attached the hangings. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/exodus-27.html

- **Gill:** The twenty pillars, each about 5 cubits apart, supported the hangings. Though some think the pillars were of shittim wood, both text and Josephus say they were bronze. Ministers of the Gospel may be specially pictured by these pillars (Prov 9:1; 1 Tim 3:15) — the principal support of the churches, set for defence of the Gospel. The silver hooks and fillets (connecting threads/rods) signify the word and ordinances administered by preachers, producing union between them and the churches. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/exodus-27.html

- **Guzik:** Ex 27:18 tells us the pillars were 7.5 ft high. Each had a bronze base and silver top with silver hooks for the linen. Silver (redemption) topped the pillars; bronze (judgment, forged in fire) provided the base — the courtyard rested on the judgment Jesus bore. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-27/

---

### vv. 12–13 — West and East Sides

**"The curtains on the west side of the courtyard shall be fifty cubits wide, with ten posts and ten bases. The east side of the courtyard, toward the sunrise, is to be fifty cubits wide."**

- **Ellicott:** The west side was half the length of the north/south sides (50 cubits), with proportionally half the pillars (10). The east side was the front, facing the sunrise — both tabernacle and Temple faced east, which Orientals regarded as "the front of the world." This belief was connected with the sun's rising but was separate from sun-worship. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/exodus-27.html

- **Gill:** The west side (the upper end, nearest the Holy of Holies) and east side (the entrance) were equal in measure — 50 cubits each, with 10 pillars and 10 sockets. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/exodus-27.html

---

### vv. 14–15 — The Two Sides of the Gate

**"Make the curtains on one side fifteen cubits long, with three posts and three bases, and the curtains on the other side fifteen cubits long, with three posts and three bases."**

- **Ellicott:** On three sides (south, west, north) there was no interruption in the hangings. On the east side the entrance broke the line. The gate curtain occupied 20 cubits out of 50, leaving 15 cubits of hangings on each side, each requiring three pillars. Thus the east side had 10 pillars total (matching the west). — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/exodus-27.html

- **Gill:** The hangings on each side of the gate were 15 cubits (7.5 yards), with three pillars and three sockets each. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/exodus-27.html

---

### v. 16 — The Gate of the Courtyard

**"The gate of the courtyard shall be twenty cubits long, with a curtain embroidered with blue, purple, and scarlet yarn, and finely spun linen. It shall have four posts and four bases."**

- **Gill:** This hanging was finer and richer than the rest — blue, purple, scarlet, and fine twined linen, wrought with needlework, the same as the door of the holy place (Ex 26:36). It is a figure of Christ, the graces of the Spirit in Him, His bloodshed, sufferings, and death — He is the door into the church and to the ordinances (Jn 10:9). The four pillars and sockets brought the total courtyard pillars to 60. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/exodus-27.html

- **Guzik:** The gate was on the east side, the same side as the tabernacle entrance. Though there was only one gate, it was large — 30 feet (10 meters) wide. It was woven from the four tabernacle colours. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-27/

- **Pulpit Commentary (Homiletics):** The gate was formed of blue, purple, and scarlet — entrance is not by man's righteousness but by bowing beneath the manifested grace of God in Christ. The court was for all Israel; living faith in Christ should be a passport to all His churches. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/exodus/27.htm

---

### vv. 17–18 — Summary of Courtyard Materials and Dimensions

**"All the posts around the courtyard shall have silver bands, silver hooks, and bronze bases. The entire courtyard shall be a hundred cubits long and fifty cubits wide, with curtains of finely spun linen five cubits high, and with bronze bases."**

- **Ellicott:** The height (5 cubits) had not been previously stated. Notably, all measurements of the tabernacle and court (except the inner covering) are either 5 cubits or multiples of 5. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/exodus-27.html

- **Gill:** The court was half the height of the tabernacle (5 cubits vs. 10), so the tabernacle could be seen above it. According to Bishop Cumberland's calculations, the court contained one rood, twenty-one perches, and twenty-seven square feet — half an Egyptian aroura. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/exodus-27.html

- **Guzik:** The court was 150 ft × 75 ft (about 50 m × 25 m). The tabernacle tent itself took up only about 7% of the courtyard area (Cole). Silver (redemption) was the foundation for the tent of meeting and the most visible part of the courtyard pillars, but the courtyard itself hung on a foundation of bronze — associated with judgment, forged in fire — picturing that the tabernacle court was founded upon the judgment Jesus took in our place. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-27/

---

### v. 19 — Bronze Utensils, Tent Pegs, and Courtyard Pegs

**"All the utensils of the tabernacle for every use, including all its tent pegs and the tent pegs of the courtyard, shall be made of bronze."**

- **Ellicott:** "All the vessels of the tabernacle" — i.e., those not already appointed to be of a richer material (cf. Ex 25:38). Bronze was the most convenient material and maintained its place even in Solomon's magnificent Temple. The "pins" (tent pegs) are now mentioned for the first time; every tent requires cords and pegs for erection. The courtyard pins were pegs employed internally and externally to keep the pillars in place, implying the use of cords. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/exodus-27.html

- **Gill:** The vessels refer either to altar utensils (repeating v.3) or to instruments used in setting up and taking down the tabernacle (hammers, etc.). The courtyard pins were brass stakes driven into the ground, with cords tied to the hangings to keep them tight against the wind (Josephus confirms this; see Isa 33:20). — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/exodus-27.html

---

### v. 20 — Pure Olive Oil for the Lamps

**"And you are to command the Israelites to bring you pure oil of pressed olives for the light, to keep the lamps burning continually."**

- **Ellicott:** This instruction had been given earlier (Ex 25:2, 6) but now with particularity. "Pure olive oil beaten" means the best oil — obtained by pounding in a mortar, free from impurities found in oil crushed in a mill. "To cause the lamp to burn always" means every night without intermission. Josephus says three lights burned day and night, but Scripture does not confirm this. The tabernacle received sufficient daylight through the linen entrance curtain. Lighting every evening is asserted in Ex 30:8; extinction in the morning appears from 1 Sam 3:3. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/exodus-27.html

- **Gill:** The command shifts to the people's responsibility to supply the oil. It had to be "pure oil olive" — not from fish or nuts, but from olives, and "beaten" (pounded in a mortar), not ground in a mill, producing the purest oil without dregs. This typified the gifts and graces of the Spirit. The lamps burned "continually" — from evening to morning, as v.21 clarifies; some Jewish writers say one lamp (the "western lamp") burned all day too. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/exodus-27.html

- **Guzik:** The oil came from pressed olives, not beaten olives. "Beaten olive oil, so the Mishnah tells us, refers to the method of production of the very best oil" (Cole). God uses pressing circumstances to produce the oil of the Holy Spirit. The saintly McCheyne urged ministers to prepare sermons with "beaten oil for the sanctuary" — truth beaten out by careful meditation. Oil uniformly symbolizes the Holy Spirit (Morgan). — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-27/

- **Precept Austin (Pulpit Commentary):** The oil was the free-will offering of the people — the light of the world springs from the consecration of believers. It was to be pure — believers must keep themselves unspotted. It was beaten, not pressed — the highest outcome of humanity is the Christ-like life. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/exodus/27.htm

---

### v. 21 — Aaron and His Sons to Tend the Lamps

**"In the Tent of Meeting, outside the veil that is in front of the Testimony, Aaron and his sons are to tend the lamps before the LORD from evening until morning. This is to be a permanent statute for the Israelites for the generations to come."**

- **Ellicott:** "Tent of Meeting" — where God met the earthly ruler of His people (Ex 25:22). "Before the Testimony" — in front of the Ark containing the Two Tables. The priestly character of Aaron and his sons, laid down in Exodus 28, is here anticipated. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/exodus-27.html

- **Gill:** Aaron and his sons tended the lamps — lighting them, dressing them, cleaning the lampstand, supplying oil, and trimming wicks. This was a "statute forever" — until the coming of the Messiah, when these shadows would pass away. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/exodus-27.html

- **Guzik:** The priests tended the lamps especially during the night. God never wanted the lamps to lose their fire. Only a continual supply of oil and trimming of wicks could keep them burning. We can only stay on fire for God if continually supplied with the oil of the Holy Spirit and "trimmed" by God. In dark days there is all the more reason to be filled with the Spirit. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-27/

- **Pulpit Commentary (Homiletics):** The lamps were to burn always — our light, the flame of love, must burn constantly before God. The lamps were tended by the ministers of God — the aim of those who labour in word and doctrine should be the development of Christ-like life, love to God and man. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/exodus/27.htm

- **Precept Austin (NET Note):** No believer can approach God apart from the altar — the sacrificial atonement must be the foundation and center of all Christian worship. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-27-commentary

---

## Points of Difference Between Traditions

### The Meaning of the Altar — Christ Himself or the Cross?

- **Reformed Baptist (Gill):** The altar is **not** the cross but **Christ Himself** — specifically His divine nature as the altar supporting and sanctifying the sacrifice of His human nature. The cross, the Lord's Table, and the heart are explicitly rejected as the antitype. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/exodus-27.html

- **Evangelical/Charismatic (Guzik):** The altar is the "killing-place" pointing to **the cross**, where Jesus died for our sins. "Our altar — our 'killing-place' — is the cross." Believers lay down their lives on that same altar (Gal 2:20; 6:14). — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-27/

- **Brethren (Grant):** The acacia wood speaks of Christ in His pure humanity; the bronze overlay speaks of Christ as the perfect expression of God's holiness ("our God is a consuming fire"). The square shape and numbers carry spiritual meaning: five = Christ taking responsibility for sin; three = resurrection. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lmg/exodus-27.html

- **Lutheran:** No distinct Lutheran commentary on this chapter was found among the searched sources from lcms.org or 1517.org.

### The "Hollow" Altar — Filled with Earth or Not?

- **Jewish commentators (Jarchi, Kalisch, followed by Ellicott and Cambridge Bible):** The hollow wooden case was filled with earth at each encampment, reconciling the acacia-wood altar with the earlier command for altars of earth or unhewn stone (Ex 20:24-25). — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/exodus-27.html ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/exodus/27.htm

- **Gill (Baptist):** Explicitly rejects the earth-filling theory as "quite contrary to the present direction." The hollowness was to make it portable and to typify Christ emptying Himself. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/exodus-27.html

### The Lamps: Night Only or Continual (Day and Night)?

- **Josephus (and some Jewish traditions):** Three of the seven lamps burned both day and night. — cited in Ellicott: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/exodus-27.html

- **Ellicott and most Protestant commentators:** "Continually" means every night, with lamps extinguished in the morning (citing Ex 30:8 and 1 Sam 3:3). The tabernacle had sufficient daylight through the linen curtain. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/exodus-27.html

- **Gill:** Says "continually" means from evening to morning, but notes some Jewish writers held that the "western lamp" burned all day as well. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/exodus-27.html

### The Grate — Inside or Outside the Altar?

- **Gill and some Jewish sources:** The grate was inside the hollow of the altar, lowered by chains from rings at the four horns, positioned midway. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/exodus-27.html

- **Cambridge Bible:** A projecting ledge ran around the altar at mid-height, supported at its outer edge by a vertical grating that rested on the ground — placing the grate **outside** as a protective screen. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/exodus/27.htm

- **Ellicott:** Admits the position is "doubtful" — either extending from the middle to the base (protecting sides from priests' feet) or surrounding the upper part (catching fallen portions). — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/exodus-27.html

---

## Other Views

### Modern Scholarship (NET Bible Notes)

- The article "the" on "altar" identifies this as the definitive high altar. The horns were "indispensable — the most sacred part" used for blood application, refuge, and intercessory prayer. The construction was a portable frame improvement over field altars — "an imagined plan to make a portable altar after the pattern of Solomon's." The courtyard was where Israelites met God, left the "world," and experienced forgiveness and worship. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-27-commentary (citing NET notes)

### Cambridge Bible (Scholarly Anglican)

- On horns: the most probable theory is that horns represent conventionalized horns of sacrificed oxen (Evans, Robertson Smith). The word "foursquare" is an archaism: "An archaism dating from a time when 'square' meant equal-sided, and it was necessary to express the number of sides" (McNeile) — citing Wesley's Journal describing an "eight square" church. Canaanite and Mycenaean parallels exist for horned altars. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/exodus/27.htm
